paragraphs: I am 藤田絢帆, and I was allowed to study at Lund University in Sweden for about eight weeks from April 2019. Before going, I left feeling anxious about my language ability and my lack of medical knowledge, but supported by the people around me, I was able to spend a very fulfilling two months. I am truly grateful to the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, beginning with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, who supported me from before departure, my friends who encouraged and stimulated me, the doctors who instructed me locally, and my parents who let me go abroad.

The city of Lund is located in southern Sweden, closer to Copenhagen than to Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, about 40 minutes by train. It is a university town where half of the population are students, a city rich in nature with forests and the sea nearby. Sweden itself is the country where English is spoken best among non-English-speaking countries, and many exchange students live in Lund, so I had no trouble with language even in daily life. Lund University is a comprehensive university that includes not only the medical school but also humanities faculties such as law and science faculties such as natural sciences, as well as students who major in art.

In the clerkship, besides medicine, of course, I was able to feel Sweden, a country that values equality even by world standards. For the first four weeks I rotated through medical oncology and for the latter four weeks the NICU, and in medical oncology I was allowed to rotate through gynecology, my chosen specialty. I was allowed to experience many internal examinations, and since it was gynecology within medical oncology, they mainly handled radiation therapy, and I was allowed to observe intravaginal irradiation. In clerkships in Japan I had seen brachytherapy only for prostate cancer in urology, so it was very interesting. I also had an opportunity to present at a journal club, where I presented on lymph node dissection in ovarian cancer, and I struggled more with the question and answer session than with the presentation itself. In the NICU I hardly did any treatment procedures, but I was allowed to do almost all the examinations by myself. There were also days when I followed nurses and nursing assistants around, and I learned about a type of care called NIDCAP. In non-intensive-care rooms such as the GCU, there were beds for parents, and it was impressive that most parents took parental leave and both were present. I felt that kangaroo care has developed from the idea that the child's family, not the medical staff, look after the child, and also that not only the mother but the father takes part, and I felt gender equality.

I also felt that there was not only gender equality but also no hierarchical relations. When a professor came in and I tried to give up my seat, the doctors told me there was no need to give up my seat, and it was impressive that in discussions people spoke regardless of age or position.

If asked whether in these two months my English ability improved markedly or my medical knowledge increased more than it would have in Japan, I think not. However, by making an effort in a new environment I was able to gain confidence and to think about my own future, and it was a very valuable two months. I had thought of Japan as a developed country until now, but when I talked in Sweden about Japan's efforts on gender equality and LGBT matters and about the cervical cancer vaccine, I came to think that this may not necessarily be so. On the other hand, when we tried Swedish folk costumes, almost nobody owned one, and I was able to appreciate anew the good side of Japan, where one's own culture is close at hand, like kimono and yukata. Also, the Swedish doctors, who value holidays and keep a balance between work and private life, had many points to learn from compared with Japan today, where work-style reform is happening. I think it was good that I could think about what kind of work-life balance I will work with in the future in a country where people work in a completely different way from Japan.

The two months of study abroad were very enjoyable, every day was out of the ordinary and fresh, and I can only be grateful that I was allowed such an experience before I started working. That I had hardly any hard times locally and could enjoy myself was thanks to the supervising doctors and my local friends. I came to want to treat the exchange students who will come to Japan from now on in the same way and to repay the kindness. I am grateful that I was allowed such a valuable experience while still a student, and I will continue to work even harder so as not to waste this experience.
Finally, I would like to express my thanks to everyone who supported my study abroad. Thank you.
